content: An otoscope, also known as an auriscope, is a medical instrument designed for examining the ears. Healthcare professionals utilize otoscopes during routine check-ups to screen for potential ear-related illnesses and to investigate symptoms involving the ears. This device enables visualization of both the outer ear and the middle ear. The otoscope is composed of two main parts: a handle and a head. The head houses an electric light source and a low-power magnifying lens. At the front end of the otoscope, there is an attachment for disposable plastic ear speculums, which are used to maintain hygiene during examinations. To begin the examination, the clinician straightens the ear canal by gently pulling on the pinna (the outer part of the ear) and then inserts the speculum end of the otoscope into the external ear canal. The examiner looks through a lens located at the rear of the instrument to inspect the ear canal and structures within. Many otoscope models feature a detachable sliding rear window, which allows the insertion of instruments through the otoscope into the ear canal. This functionality is particularly useful for procedures such as removing earwax (cerumen). Additionally, most otoscopes include a port for attaching a bulb that can deliver a puff of air through the speculum. This air puff is used to assess the mobility of the tympanic membrane (eardrum), which is an important diagnostic test. Otoscopes are available in two primary forms: wall-mounted and portable. Wall-mounted otoscopes are connected to a base unit via a flexible power cord. The base unit serves as a holder for the otoscope when not in use and provides a source of electric power, as it is plugged into an electrical outlet. Portable otoscopes, on the other hand, are battery-powered, with the batteries typically housed in the handle. These batteries are often rechargeable and can be recharged using a base unit. Otoscopes are frequently sold as part of a diagnostic set, which often includes an ophthalmoscope for examining the eyes. Common conditions that can be diagnosed using an otoscope include otitis media (infection of the middle ear) and otitis externa (infection of the outer ear). Beyond ear examinations, otoscopes are also commonly used to inspect patients' noses, eliminating the need for a separate nasal speculum. Furthermore, with the speculum removed, otoscopes can be employed to examine the upper throat.
